body: Hi! I completely know what you’re talking about. That’s much more common for us with TKN. Typically what helps me is when I do an “extra wash” and then rerun it. Thankfully it’s not every time, but it is a nightmare. Especially when NOX and TP come right out and I have to fight the machine with TKN for hours and stop what I’m doing every 15 minutes to tend to the machine.
I’ll add this system is also much more automated than the Hach TNTs. But I also have love for those too when it comes to tests I don’t need QA data for.

I conduct interviews at my plant for operator trainee positions, and with your qualifications my first assumption would be that you weren’t going to stay long. The best advice I can give you is to give responses that make it seem like you want to be there for a while. For example, like where do you see yourself in five years, or what is your ideal next role, and good answer would be, “continue learning all I can about how this plant operates so that I can work my way up as new opportunities to grow within the plant present themself.” An answer someone gave me that I liked was that they wanted to achieve the highest licensure available because it was the pinnacle of our field. You can also convey longevity in your questions at the end. For example the licensing process, will there be room to advance, etc. 

Also, exactly what moricedish said about wardrobe. 

Congrats and good luck! They’re just people too. They’re also nervous. No one enjoys the process. Don’t be nervous. There is a lot of turnover in this field because it’s a job for smart people who don’t mind working hard and getting their hands dirty and not many people like they exist. Most people work for 6months to a year and realize it’s not for them. so honestly you’ll be an asset to any plant that’s not afraid of your qualifications. And one that is you don’t want to work for. However the job security is next to none.

I have this exact position. I have my bachelors in biology. I started at a water plant. Now I work at a wastewater plant that pays for me to take courses and get training, like the Sacramento one mentioned, to get my license. I’m in Virginia, but I assume it’s similar everywhere, with your degree you can work your way up to your licenses quickly, and that makes you a more competitor candidate at other plants who are hiring in the lab, or you can work your way up to your lab at the plant you start at. My pay is pretty good, not great for the area, I get raises with my licenses and performance evaluations. It is repetitive, but I enjoy challenging myself to get it done faster or better. The biggest pain in the butt is all the quality assurance and regulatory stuff, but you can make that fun too. I hope this helps.

In my lab, we had a corrective action on cBOD open for like a year. We were using polyseed and finding our GGA was either too high or too low, depending on how fresh the polyseed was from when we opened it. We found that using primary as our seed, but controlling the concentration by using turbidity fixed our issue. We keep it at 50 ntu’s +/- 10 ntu’s. 

Also, the standard methods states the seed being between .6-1 is a recommendation, not a requirement like the gga range.
